title: Pride And Prejudice: CHAPTER XLIII
enhanced_title: The Gardens of Pemberley: A Chapter of Revelation and Transformation
author: Jane Austen
description: Elizabeth Bennet's first visit to Pemberley, where she discovers Darcy's true character through the testimony of his housekeeper and encounters the man himself in a manner strikingly altered from their previous meetings.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's initial approach to Pemberley is marked by nervous anticipation, watching for the woods with 'perturbation' and experiencing 'high flutter' in her spirits. This emotional volatility reveals her complex feelings about Darcy—not simple aversion, but something deeper and more conflicted that she has not fully acknowledged to herself. The very landscape seems to mirror her inner state, drawing her forward even as propriety and pride counsel retreat.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: her spirits were in a high flutter.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The description of Pemberley House as where 'natural beauty had been so little counteracted by an awkward taste' serves as powerful symbolism. Elizabeth realizes that Darcy's character, like his estate, possesses a natural dignity and refinement that belies her earlier judgment of him as artificial and proud. The phrase 'to be mistress of Pemberley might be something' veils deeper, unacknowledged longing.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: to be mistress of Pemberley might be something!

analysis_entries.paragraph: The housekeeper Mrs. Reynolds becomes a crucial narrative device, offering testimony that contradicts Elizabeth's established opinion of Darcy. When she speaks of his sweet temper, generosity, and excellent treatment of servants and tenants, Elizabeth is forced to confront that her prejudice has distorted her perception of his true character. The moment of recognition is crystallized when Elizabeth almost stares at the housekeeper and silently asks herself whether this can truly be the same man she has so long misjudged.

The unexpected encounter by the stables represents a pivotal moment of dramatic irony. Elizabeth, who had believed herself safe from encountering Darcy, must face him in circumstances that might seem like deliberate pursuit. Their mutual blushing and discomfort reveal suppressed feelings that polite society demands be constrained, and the few minutes they spend together become, for Elizabeth, some of the most uncomfortable of her life.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
the few
minutes in which they continued together were some of the most
uncomfortable of her life.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Darcy's transformation in manner—from 'haughty' to 'gentle,' from 'proud' to 'civil'—suggests either genuine character development or Elizabeth's altered perception. The contrast with his behavior at Rosings, where he delivered his proposal with such arrogance, is striking and disorienting for Elizabeth. She turns the question over repeatedly, unable to settle on an explanation, as his every sentence increases her astonishment and her embarrassment in equal measure.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
She knew not what to think, or how to
account for it.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The invitation to meet Georgiana represents the highest compliment Darcy can offer, as his sister represents his most treasured relationship. Elizabeth immediately recognizes that whatever desire Miss Darcy might have of being acquainted with her must be the work of her brother, acknowledging the active role Darcy plays in his sister's social connections. This gesture signals that his resentment has not curdled into contempt, and that his regard for Elizabeth persists despite her rejection.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
it was gratifying to know that his resentment had not made
him think really ill of her.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The Gardiners' favorable assessment of Darcy provides external validation that Elizabeth's transformed opinion is not merely wishful thinking. Their discernment—seeing him as 'perfectly well-behaved, polite, and unassuming'—confirms that his behavior is genuinely altered, not simply a product of Elizabeth's changed perception. Elizabeth's silent recognition that they have entirely mistaken his character marks her own quiet, private vindication of the man she is beginning to love.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Elizabeth felt that they had entirely mistaken his character, but said
nothing.

quote_entries.quote: There is also one other person in the party who more particularly wishes to be known to you. Will you allow me, or do I ask too much, to introduce my sister to your acquaintance during your stay at Lambton?

quote_entries.quote: The occurrences of the day were too full of interest to leave Elizabeth much attention for any of these new friends; and she could do nothing but think, and think with wonder, of Mr. Darcy's civility, and, above all, of his wishing her to be acquainted with his sister.
